summary: A humorous Polygon field guide that assesses whether famous vampire authors were themselves secretly vampires, tracing English-language vampire fiction from Polidori and Stoker to King, Rice, Hamilton, and Waititi. Each entry names a best-known work, explains how vampire stories reflected their era, and ends with a tongue-in-cheek verdict. The piece also sketches the genre's shift from terror to sexy camp to comedy.
one_line: A tongue-in-cheek Polygon guide rating vampire authors from Polidori to Taika Waititi on whether they were secretly vampires.
key_facts: John William Polidori wrote The Vampyre (1819), born from the Swiss chalet spooky story contest where Mary Shelley conceived Frankenstein.
Lord Byron passed his vampire story idea to his personal physician Polidori, who wrote the novel three years later; Lord Ruthven is read as a stand-in for Byron.
Verdict on Polidori: not a vampire, but Byron is 'vampire all the way'.
Bram Stoker published Dracula in 1897 and was born to a middle-class Protestant Irish family in the 1840s; he was interested in the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and the Freemasons.
Stephen King's 'Salem's Lot (1975) was his second published book after Carrie (1974) and reflects post-Watergate suspicions of government corruption.
Verdict on Stephen King: Vampire (complimentary), citing his rural New England life, surviving a car hit, and stances against corporate power and for trans rights.
Anne Rice's Interview with the Vampire (1976) was the first mainstream book to prominently feature gay, campy, unapologetically fabulous vampires; The Vampire Chronicles ran 1976-2018.
Rice left Catholicism, returned in the early 2000s to write Christ-themed fiction, then rejected the Church again; verdict: not a vampire.
Laurell K. Hamilton's Anita Blake: Vampire Hunter series (1993-present) is compared to a 1970s grindhouse flick; verdict: not a vampire, but 'a good punchline'.
Taika Waititi co-created What We Do in the Shadows with Jemaine Clement; the two wrote and directed the original 2014 movie, and the series has run since 2019.
Verdict on Taika Waititi: Dracula, described as the vampires' king.
